Rain made this glacier slide seven and a half metres in a single day.
That's more than double its speed.
This week, scientists studying Turner Glacier in Alaska showed how it happens.
They pinned GPS to the ice and logged its position every fifteen seconds. Nine of sixteen big rainstorms sent it racing.
But how can rain speed up ice? It doesn't push from above. It sneaks underneath.
Rainwater pours down cracks and holes, all the way to the rock at the bottom.
The drains under the ice can't carry it away fast enough. So the water pressure builds, and the ice loses its grip.
Less friction, more slide. About twelve hours after the rain began, the glacier sped up. Within two weeks, it calmed down.
So it's not only heat that moves a glacier. Sometimes, a storm is the grease underneath.
